questions.scenario: An HR analyst at a 400-person company wants Claude to find themes in free-text answers from the annual engagement survey. Before uploading, she deletes the respondent name column. The export still contains department, job title, years of service and office location for every answer. Several departments have fewer than five people, and policy allows only anonymized employee data in the company's Claude workspace.
questions.stem: Which step would MOST effectively bring this upload in line with the policy while keeping the analysis useful?

options.text: Upload the file as it is, since deleting the name column already makes the responses anonymous
Broaden or drop the fields that could single people out, such as merging small departments and removing title, tenure and office location
Add an instruction asking Claude never to mention departments, job titles or locations in its theme summary
Replace each department name with a numeric code but leave the title, tenure and location columns in place

questions.explanation: Removing names is only the first step. In a department of three people, a job title combined with tenure and location can point to one individual just as reliably as a name, so the data is not yet anonymized. Merging small units and dropping fields the theme analysis does not need removes these **indirect identifiers**. The comment text is kept, so the analysis still works and the upload meets the policy.

whyWrong.A: A title plus tenure in a three-person team can identify someone just as well as a name. The data is still personal data.
whyWrong.C: An instruction changes what Claude writes in its summary. It does nothing about what was uploaded, and the uploaded data is what the policy restricts.
whyWrong.D: A code for the department changes nothing. The combination of title, tenure and location can still single people out.

questions.mindset: Anonymized means no one can be singled out, not just that the name column is gone.

questions.scenario: An accounts-payable specialist wants Claude to flag duplicate or unusual vendor invoices from last quarter. The export includes vendor name, invoice number, date, amount, and each vendor's bank account and routing numbers. Policy treats banking details as restricted.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to prepare the file?

options.text: Upload the full export so Claude has every field it could use to spot fraud
Upload the full export and ask Claude to ignore the bank account columns
Skip Claude and review the invoices by hand, since financial data is involved
Delete the banking columns first, since duplicate checks need only the other fields

questions.explanation: This is **data minimization**: share only what the task needs. Vendor, invoice number, date and amount are enough to find duplicates and outliers. The restricted bank details add no value to this analysis, so the right step is to remove them before upload. The work still gets done, within policy.

whyWrong.A: More data is not better when the extra fields are restricted and the task doesn't need them. This uploads data the policy protects.
whyWrong.B: Asking Claude to ignore a column doesn't undo the upload. The restricted data has already been shared.
whyWrong.C: This throws away a useful analysis. A minimized file meets the policy and still lets Claude help.

questions.mindset: Before you upload, ask what fields the task actually needs and remove the rest.

questions.scenario: A paralegal at a law firm uses the firm's Claude Team workspace. The firm's owners have enabled a cloud-drive connector. The paralegal's drive account can open every client matter folder in the firm, including matters she doesn't work on. She wants Claude to summarize the documents in one matter folder for an attorney.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements BEST describe how she should handle data exposure in this task? Choose TWO.

options.text: Point Claude at the specific matter folder or files the task needs, not the whole drive, so other clients' material stays out of the chat
The connector only reaches files the firm has marked for AI use, so nothing outside the matter can come into the chat
Tell Claude in the prompt to look only at the one matter, because that instruction limits what the connector is able to open
The connector can reach whatever her own drive account can open, so her broad access means broad exposure if she searches loosely
Download the folder and upload it to a personal Claude account instead, which keeps the firm's drive out of the process entirely

questions.explanation: Claude's connectors follow the permissions of the source system: if the user can open a file there, the connector can reach it, and if she can't, it can't. Her account is very broad, so a loose search could pull other clients' confidential documents into the chat. The right habits are to **scope the request** to the folder or files the task needs, and to understand that her own access sets the limit of what Claude can reach.

whyWrong.B: Connectors don't use an 'AI-approved' label. They mirror what the user can already open in the source system.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction steers what Claude tries to do. It isn't an access control and doesn't change the connector's permissions.
whyWrong.E: Moving client documents to a personal account breaks the approved-tools rule and removes the firm's data protections.

questions.mindset: A connector sees what you can see, so scope each request to what the task needs.

questions.scenario: A compensation manager on a Claude Team plan set up a Project to draft offer letters. She uploaded the company's confidential salary-band spreadsheet as Project knowledge. A month later she learns that a colleague set the Project's visibility so everyone in the organization can view and use it.

options.text: Restrict the Project to invited members only, review who has access, and report the exposure if policy requires it
Add a Project instruction telling Claude not to reveal salary figures to anyone outside the compensation team
Leave the setting alone, since anyone in the organization is an internal employee bound by confidentiality
Delete the Project and every offer letter template, then rebuild everything later in a new Project

questions.explanation: On Team and Enterprise plans, a Project can be private to invited members or visible across the organization, and anyone who can use the Project can draw on its knowledge. Making the Project invite-only closes the exposure, and reviewing members keeps access to those who need it. If policy treats wider access to confidential pay data as an incident, she should also report it.

whyWrong.B: Claude can't tell who is asking, and an instruction isn't access control. Anyone who can use the Project can still reach the spreadsheet.
whyWrong.C: Confidential pay data is restricted inside the company too. Being an employee doesn't mean someone needs to see it.
whyWrong.D: This overreacts and loses work. Fixing the visibility setting removes the exposure without destroying the templates.

questions.mindset: Project knowledge is visible to everyone who can use the Project, so control who's in it.

questions.scenario: A consultant used the firm's Claude Enterprise workspace to analyze a client's customer-churn data and wants to show the findings to the client's project lead, who works for another company. The chat contains rows of the client's customer records.

options.text: Create a share link to the full chat and email it, since the data belongs to the client anyway
Add the client's project lead to the firm's workspace for a week so they can read the chat
Write up the findings as a separate deliverable, check it for record-level data, and send it through the firm's approved channel
Copy the full chat transcript into a document so the client can see exactly how the analysis was done

questions.explanation: The client needs the findings, not the working chat with raw customer records in it. A separate deliverable lets the consultant share only what's needed, review it for anything identifying, and send it through the channel the firm approves for client work. As a secondary point, sharing in organization workspaces is built for members, not external readers, so a chat link wasn't the right mechanism anyway.

whyWrong.A: A share link would hand over raw customer records and the full working history, not just the findings. More data than the client needs is still more exposure than allowed.
whyWrong.B: Adding an outsider to the workspace to get around sharing limits is an access workaround. It may also expose other client work.
whyWrong.D: Pasting the transcript sends the same raw records outside the firm. It just uses a different file.

questions.mindset: Share the findings, not the working session, and review them before they leave the building.

questions.scenario: A team lead at a health insurer proposes a new team rule: "Anything containing member information must be done in an incognito chat." Company policy says member health data may not be entered into Claude unless it has been de-identified.
questions.stem: What is the BEST response to the proposal?

options.text: Adopt it, since incognito chats are deleted immediately when the window closes and so leave nothing behind
Point out that incognito only keeps a chat out of history and memory, so de-identification is still required first
Adopt it, and also tell Claude at the start of each incognito chat that the content is confidential
Replace it with a rule that member data may only be used in Claude on the team lead's own account

questions.explanation: Incognito chats aren't saved to chat history and aren't drawn on by memory, but that only changes what is kept afterwards. The policy's question is **whether** member health data may be entered at all, and the answer is only after de-identification. Incognito is a privacy convenience, not a permission: it doesn't change what you're allowed to share.

whyWrong.A: This misstates how incognito works — its promise is about history and memory, not instant erasure. Even if chats were wiped on close, deleting after the fact wouldn't make policy-restricted data allowed.
whyWrong.C: Telling Claude the data is confidential doesn't change how it's handled or what the policy allows.
whyWrong.D: Moving data to one person's account adds no protection and is no more compliant. The data still isn't de-identified.

questions.mindset: Incognito changes what's saved to your history. It doesn't change what you're allowed to share.

questions.scenario: A marketing agency has an approved Claude Team workspace that policy allows for confidential client material. A new retail client's services contract includes a clause saying the agency may not process the client's customer data with third-party AI services without the client's written consent. An account executive wants Claude to segment the client's loyalty-program members for a campaign.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed in the approved workspace, since the agency's own policy already allows confidential client material there
Proceed, but remove names and emails first, since de-identified rows are no longer the client's customer data
Drop the segmentation idea and tell the client the agency can't use AI on their account
Raise the clause with the account owner or legal to get written consent, and work only with non-customer material until then

questions.explanation: Regulatory and privacy obligations can come from **contracts** as well as from laws and internal policy, and the strictest applicable rule governs. The agency's general permission doesn't override a specific promise made to this client. The right move is to route the question to the people who own the client relationship and the contract to obtain consent, while continuing work that doesn't touch customer data. That keeps the project moving without breaching the contract.

whyWrong.A: Internal policy sets a floor, not a ceiling. A stricter client contract still applies to that client's data.
whyWrong.B: Deciding alone that stripped rows fall outside the clause is a legal interpretation the account executive isn't entitled to make, and loyalty or purchase histories can still identify people.
whyWrong.C: This gives up too early. Written consent is a normal, achievable route, and the clause explicitly anticipates it.

questions.mindset: The strictest applicable rule wins, and contracts with clients count as rules.

questions.scenario: A customer-success manager pseudonymizes support tickets by replacing customer names with codes such as "CUST-0412" before analyzing them in a shared Claude Project. To make follow-up easier, she plans to upload the lookup table that maps each code to the real customer name as Project knowledge too.

options.text: Keep the lookup table outside Claude in an access-controlled location, and match codes to names only when follow-up is needed
Upload the lookup table but tell Claude in the Project instructions never to reveal real names in its answers
Upload the lookup table in a separate chat in the same Project so that it stays apart from the tickets
Skip the codes and upload the original tickets, since the table would make them identifiable anyway

questions.explanation: Pseudonymization only protects people if the key that reverses it is kept apart from the coded data. If the table sits inside the Project, everyone with access to the Project can re-identify every customer, which undoes the safeguard. Keeping the key outside Claude, with restricted access, lets the analysis run on coded data and keeps re-identification under deliberate human control.

whyWrong.B: The mapping would still be in the Project for everyone with access. An instruction to Claude doesn't protect data that has already been shared.
whyWrong.C: Knowledge in a shared Project is available across its chats, so the coded data and the key still end up together for every Project member.
whyWrong.D: This gives up a safeguard that works. Kept separate, the key doesn't make the coded tickets identifiable inside Claude.

questions.mindset: A pseudonym only protects people while the key is kept somewhere else.

questions.scenario: A product designer wants Claude's feedback on the layout of an internal admin dashboard and plans to upload a full-screen screenshot. The screenshot's side panel shows real customers' names, emails and recent orders.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to get the feedback?

options.text: Upload the screenshot as it is, since Claude is being asked about layout rather than customer data
Upload the screenshot and ask Claude to disregard any personal information it can see
Crop or blur the customer panel, or capture the screen with sample data, before uploading
Describe the layout in words only, since images of internal tools should never be shared with AI

questions.explanation: Images count as data too. Everything visible in a screenshot is shared when you upload it, whatever the question is about. The layout review doesn't need real customer details, so cropping, blurring or recapturing with sample data minimizes exposure and keeps the visual feedback that makes the review useful.

whyWrong.A: What you're asking about doesn't limit what you share. The customer details are uploaded either way.
whyWrong.B: Asking Claude to disregard the details doesn't undo the upload. The personal data has already been shared.
whyWrong.D: A blanket ban gives up useful visual feedback. A cleaned-up screenshot is safe and works better.

questions.mindset: Everything in the file gets shared, so clean up images the same way you trim spreadsheets.

questions.scenario: A university student-support adviser uses the institution's Claude Enterprise workspace, where memory is turned on. She wants help drafting a support plan for a student who has disclosed a mental-health condition. Policy allows de-identified case details in the workspace for drafting, but says sensitive case information must not be kept in AI tools beyond the task.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions BEST meet the policy while still letting her get help with the plan? Choose TWO.

options.text: Include the student's name and ID so Claude can link this plan to earlier conversations about the same case
Describe the case in de-identified terms, such as year of study and needs, without names, IDs or unique details
Tell Claude at the end of the chat to forget everything it learned about the student's condition
Paste the full case file, then delete the chat afterwards so no sensitive information remains anywhere
Use an incognito chat, or turn memory off for this chat, so the details aren't carried into later chats

questions.explanation: Two separate risks are involved. **What is shared:** de-identifying the case meets the policy's condition for using the workspace at all. **What persists:** with memory on, context can carry into later chats, against the policy's instruction not to keep sensitive case information beyond the task. An incognito chat, or switching memory off before the first message, keeps the details out of memory. Together these let her draft the plan within policy.

whyWrong.A: Adding identifiers goes against the policy's de-identification condition and makes it more likely that sensitive context persists.
whyWrong.C: This asks for deletion after the details have already been captured. The policy expects prevention — de-identify up front and keep the chat out of memory — and an in-chat request isn't a dependable way to purge stored context.
whyWrong.D: The full case file breaks the de-identification rule as soon as it's pasted. Deleting the chat later doesn't make that compliant.

questions.mindset: Control what you share (de-identify) and what persists (memory settings) separately.

questions.scenario: Told to anonymize a year of retail returns data before using Claude to find out why returns rose, an analyst replaced every value except the return reason with "[REDACTED]", including dates, product categories and store regions. Claude's analysis came back vague and generic.
questions.stem: What should the analyst do NEXT?

options.text: Switch to a more capable model, since a stronger model can find patterns in the redacted text
Upload the original unredacted file, since the redacted version has proven useless for the task
Give Claude more examples of good analyses, since the problem is the prompt rather than the data
Restore the non-identifying fields the analysis needs, keeping only customer identifiers removed

questions.explanation: Minimization means removing what isn't needed, not removing everything. Dates, product categories and regions don't identify customers, and they're exactly what a trend analysis depends on. The aim is to **remove identifiers and keep the analytic fields**. That keeps the file compliant and makes the analysis useful again.

whyWrong.A: A bigger model can't recover information that isn't in the file. The problem is missing data, not model capability.
whyWrong.B: Going back to the full file overcorrects and brings customer identifiers back. A targeted redaction fixes the real issue.
whyWrong.C: Examples can't make up for missing fields. Without dates or categories there are no trends to find.

questions.mindset: Minimize to what the task needs: strip identifiers, keep the analytic signal.

questions.scenario: A nonprofit's program officer used the approved Claude workspace to summarize de-identified feedback from 60 participants in a small rural job-training program. The summary will go into a public annual report. It includes a direct quote: "As the only welder in the program who is also raising twins, I nearly quit in week three."
questions.stem: Which TWO steps should she take before the summary is published? Choose TWO.

options.text: Publish it as is, because the source data was de-identified before Claude ever saw it
Ask Claude to confirm that the summary contains no personal data, and publish if it says so
Review the output for details that could single out a participant, such as unique roles or life circumstances
Add a note to the report saying all participant data was processed anonymously by AI
Paraphrase or generalize the quote so the point survives but the person cannot be recognized

questions.explanation: De-identifying the input doesn't guarantee the output is safe. A verbatim quote can carry identifying details, and in a small local program "the only welder raising twins" points to one person. A human review of the output for re-identification risk, followed by paraphrasing or generalizing the risky detail, protects the participant and keeps the insight for the report.

whyWrong.A: The output brought back an identifying detail from the comment text. Removing names from the input wasn't enough.
whyWrong.B: Claude's own check isn't a reliable control. It also can't judge local context, such as how few welders the program has.
whyWrong.D: A note about the process does nothing to protect the participant the quote still identifies.

questions.mindset: Check the output for privacy too, because identifying details can come back in quotes.

questions.scenario: An employee wellness coordinator wants to use Claude to plan next year's wellness program. She has two possible inputs: a spreadsheet of individual employees' health-claim records, and an aggregated report from the benefits provider showing claim categories as percentages by age band, with no individual rows. Company policy forbids entering employee health records into any AI tool and names the privacy officer as the contact for exceptions.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Use the aggregated provider report as Claude's input, since it supports planning without individual health records
Use the individual records but strip names, since health claims without names are no longer health records
If finer detail seems necessary, ask the privacy officer before using anything beyond the aggregated report
Upload the individual records in an incognito chat, so nothing about employees' health is kept afterwards
Ask Claude whether the company policy allows health claim data, and follow its interpretation

questions.explanation: Program planning needs trends, not individuals. The aggregated report gives Claude what it needs and contains no individual health records, so it stays within the policy. If the coordinator thinks she needs more detail, the policy names who decides exceptions: the privacy officer. Choosing the **least sensitive input that does the job** and **escalating to the policy owner** when unsure are both core data-governance habits.

whyWrong.B: Individual claim rows are still health records about real people, and combinations of claim details, treatments and dates can point to individuals even without names. The policy bans them outright.
whyWrong.D: Incognito controls history and memory, not what you may share. The policy forbids entering these records at all.
whyWrong.E: Claude is not the authority on your company's policy. The policy names a human owner for exactly these questions.

questions.mindset: Pick the least sensitive input that does the job, and take exceptions to the policy owner.

questions.scenario: An operations lead at an online retailer wants Claude to help draft replies to customer complaints. The team works from call transcripts, and customers sometimes read their full payment card number aloud during calls. Company policy prohibits payment card numbers being entered into any AI tool.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way for the team to proceed?

options.text: Paste the transcripts as they are, because the card numbers are already stored in the company's own systems
Add a masking or redaction step for card numbers before transcripts are pasted, and keep that step in the standard workflow
Paste the transcripts and instruct Claude never to repeat or store any card numbers it sees
Enter the transcripts in smaller batches so that any single chat contains only a few card numbers

questions.explanation: The policy bans card numbers entering the tool at all, so the fix must sit **before entry**. A masking or redaction step that runs on every transcript is a deterministic control: it keeps the workflow compliant even under time pressure, and the drafting task still works because complaint replies never need the numbers. A prompt instruction acts only after the data is already shared, and batching limits how much is shared, not whether it is shared.

whyWrong.A: The policy restricts entering card numbers into AI tools. What the company already stores elsewhere doesn't create permission to paste it into Claude.
whyWrong.C: An instruction changes what Claude says next, not what has already been entered. The prohibited data is in the conversation from the moment it is pasted.
whyWrong.D: Fewer numbers per chat still means entering card numbers. The policy sets a limit on the data itself, not on how much appears at a time.

questions.mindset: A control that stops restricted data at the point of entry beats an instruction or a volume limit applied afterwards.

questions.scenario: An executive assistant is asked to turn a document labeled "Confidential: Board Members Only" into a one-page brief. Company policy allows internal and confidential documents in the Claude workspace but excludes anything marked board-restricted unless the corporate secretary approves.

options.text: Upload it, since the workspace is approved for confidential material and board papers are a type of confidential document
Upload it to a private Project only the assistant can see, so the board material stays protected from others
Ask the corporate secretary for approval first, and write the brief without Claude if approval isn't given
Retype the main points into the chat instead of uploading the file, so the document itself is never shared

questions.explanation: Data classification labels decide what may go where. This document carries a more restrictive label than general confidential material, and the policy names who can approve an exception. Getting that approval, or doing the work without Claude, follows the rule. Reading the general permission as if it covered the specific exclusion does not.

whyWrong.A: This ignores the specific exclusion. The narrower rule for board material overrides the general permission for confidential documents.
whyWrong.B: A private Project limits who else can see the file, but the policy restricts putting it into the AI tool at all.
whyWrong.D: Retyping the content is a workaround. The restricted information still goes into Claude, just in a different form.

questions.mindset: Read the label, follow the most specific rule, and get approval from the named owner.
